elements.element: Customer owns Deliverables and work product created for Customer.
elements.evidence: Revised 14.2: "Customer exclusively owns every Deliverable created for Customer"; "Deliverable" is defined in 1.4 to cover reports, configurations, designs and other work product created specifically for Customer.

elements.element: Vendor assigns the Deliverables and work product to Customer.
elements.evidence: Revised 14.2: "Vendor hereby assigns to Customer all right, title, and interest in each Deliverable" — a present-tense operative assignment.

elements.element: Vendor retains its pre-existing intellectual property.
elements.evidence: 14.3 "Vendor retains Vendor Technology", and 1.8 defines Vendor Technology as Vendor's pre-existing software, tools, models, templates and technology; unchanged by the edit.

elements.element: Customer's licence to Vendor IP embedded in Deliverables is perpetual.
elements.evidence: 13.2 grants a "perpetual" licence for Vendor Technology "embedded in a Deliverable"; 14.3 confirms the 13.2 licence applies to Vendor Technology incorporated in or required to use a Deliverable.

elements.element: Customer's licence to embedded Vendor IP is irrevocable.
elements.evidence: 13.2: "perpetual, irrevocable, worldwide, royalty-free, fully paid licence" for material embedded in a Deliverable.

elements.element: Customer's licence to embedded Vendor IP is royalty-free.
elements.evidence: 13.2: "royalty-free, fully paid licence" covering Vendor Technology embedded in a Deliverable.

elements.element: Customer retains all rights in Customer Data.
elements.evidence: 14.1: "As between the Parties, Customer owns all Customer Data, Customer Confidential Information, Customer-provided material..."; no assignment of Customer Data to Vendor remains anywhere in the rendered text.

elements.element: Any Vendor licence in Customer Data is limited to processing it solely to provide the Services.
elements.evidence: 14.1: "No right transfers to Vendor except the limited right to process that material solely to provide, secure, support, and improve the Services for Customer." Securing, supporting and improving the Services for Customer is service delivery, not independent exploitation; no resale, distribution or wider-purpose right is granted.

elements.element: The parties do not jointly own intellectual property.
elements.evidence: 14.4: "No jointly owned intellectual property is created unless the Parties sign a separate instrument identifying it and their exploitation rights." The default is no joint ownership and any exception requires a future signed instrument that fixes exploitation rights, so no standing joint-ownership regime exists.

elements.element: Vendor may retain ownership of generic tools and know-how.
elements.evidence: 14.3 retains Vendor Technology to Vendor, and 1.4 excludes from Deliverables "generally applicable ideas, methods, skills, and know-how retained in the unaided memory of Vendor personnel."

elements.element: Customer's licence to Deliverables is perpetual.
elements.evidence: After the edit Customer owns the Deliverables outright (14.2), so no Customer licence to Deliverables is granted; the 13.2 perpetual licence reaches only software and Vendor Technology. Literally unmet, but moot because the preferred ownership element is satisfied.

elements.element: Customer's licence to Deliverables is irrevocable.
elements.evidence: No Deliverable licence exists in the rendered text; 13.2's irrevocable licence is limited to "software and Vendor Technology". Superseded by outright Customer ownership under 14.2.

elements.element: Customer's licence to Deliverables is worldwide.
elements.evidence: No Deliverable licence clause remains; the worldwide wording in 13.2 attaches only to Vendor Technology/software. Rendered moot by the ownership fix.

elements.element: Customer's licence to Deliverables is royalty-free.
elements.evidence: No Deliverable licence remains after the edit; royalty-free wording in 13.2 covers only Vendor Technology and delivered software.

elements.element: Customer may use and modify Deliverables for its business.
elements.evidence: No express use/modify licence to Deliverables appears; the right now flows from ownership in 14.2 rather than from a licence grant, so the fallback element as drafted is not literally present.

elements.element: Customer may sublicense Deliverables for its business.
elements.evidence: No sublicensing language for Deliverables appears in the rendered text; the fallback checklist is therefore incomplete even though ownership confers broader rights.

elements.element: Any Vendor licence in Customer Data is limited to processing it solely to provide the Services.
elements.evidence: 14.1 confines Vendor to "the limited right to process that material solely to provide, secure, support, and improve the Services for Customer" with no resale, distribution or broader-purpose right.

reasons: The preferred checklist is position-complete: the single edit to 14.2 supplies Customer ownership plus an express present-tense assignment of each Deliverable, and the remaining preferred elements are already satisfied by retained 13.2 (perpetual, irrevocable, royalty-free embedded-IP licence), 14.1 (Customer Data ownership with processing limited to service delivery), 14.3 (Vendor retains Vendor Technology) and 14.4 (no joint ownership).

The fallback level is not complete because the four Deliverable-licence attributes and the use/modify/sublicense rights are not expressed anywhere; that is immaterial since the preferred level is met and ownership is the stronger outcome, but the finding should not be characterised as resting on the fallback.

Minimal: the edit replaces only the two offending sentences of 14.2 (Vendor exclusive ownership; revocable, non-transferable, term-limited licence) and adds nothing outside the checklist — no survival tail, no expense or procedure language, no duplication of the 13.2 licence.

Preserves intent: 14.3's cross-reference to the Section 13.2 perpetual licence and 13.2's "embedded in a Deliverable" trigger both still operate; Vendor's identification and third-party-material restrictions, the feedback mechanics in 14.4 and the 1.4/1.8 definitions are untouched, leaving no dangling reference or contradictory retained sentence.
Deterministic gates are consistent with substance: no assignment of Customer IP or Customer Data to Vendor survives, and the operation is the shortest route to a complete level.

Classification of the original clause as a deviation is correct — original 14.2 gave Vendor exclusive ownership of paid-for Deliverables with only a revocable, non-transferable, term-limited licence back, failing even the fallback.
